passages.t: Pharaoh the great monster, and the splintered reed
passages.happening:
In the tenth year, God speaks against Pharaoh, ‘O great monster who lies among his rivers’, who claims to have made the Nile himself (verse 3). God will put hooks in his jaws, haul him out with the fish of his rivers, and leave him in the open field for the birds and beasts (verses 4-5). ‘For you were only a staff of reeds to the house of Israel’ (verse 6). When Israel leaned on Egypt, it splintered and wrenched their backs (verse 7).

God will make Egypt a desolate ruin from Migdol to Syene for forty years and scatter the Egyptians among the nations (verses 9-12). Then he will bring them back to Pathros, ‘There they will be a lowly kingdom’ (verse 14). ‘Egypt will never again be an object of trust for the house of Israel’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The date is January 587 BC, about a year into the siege of Jerusalem. The Pharaoh was Hophra, called Apries by Greek writers. Jeremiah records that an Egyptian army marched out during the siege, the Babylonians briefly withdrew, and then the Egyptians went home. That is probably the splintered reed. An Assyrian official had used the same picture a century earlier to mock Hezekiah's trust in Egypt.

The Nile was Egypt's life, and Pharaoh was regarded as a divine king who kept the world in order, the river's flood included. The great monster is probably the crocodile, but the word is also used for the sea dragon of chaos. To be left unburied was a horror everywhere, and above all in Egypt, where burial was central to religion. Migdol to Syene means from the northern frontier to Aswan in the far south; Pathros is Upper Egypt.
passages.later: An Assyrian official called Egypt ‘that splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it’ (2 Kings 18:21). Jeremiah told Zedekiah that Pharaoh's army ‘will go back to its own land’ (Jeremiah 37:7).
passages.hard:
Was Egypt ever desolate for forty years, as verses 11 to 13 say?

No period is known in which Egypt lay uninhabited for forty years, and readers who take the Bible seriously answer in more than one way. Many understand forty years as a round, symbolic number, a generation of punishment like Israel's forty years in the wilderness and the forty years of Judah's guilt in 4:6; Egypt, like Israel, would suffer a time of judgment and then be restored in a lowered state. Others point to Babylonian and later Persian invasions of Egypt and the deportation of Egyptians, and see a looser fulfillment.

The firmest part of the prophecy is its end. Egypt did cease to be a great imperial power, and after the Persian conquest in 525 BC it was ruled by foreign dynasties, Persian, Greek and Roman, for most of the centuries that followed. The chapter's focus is less on a timetable than on Egypt as a lowly kingdom that Israel would never again trust.
passages.asks: Pharaoh claimed to have made the Nile. Ask what you take credit for that was given to you. And ask what you lean on that might splinter.

passages.happening: In the twenty-seventh year comes the latest word in the book. ‘Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon caused his army to labor strenuously against Tyre. Every head was made bald and every shoulder made raw. But he and his army received no wages from Tyre for the labor they expended on it’ (verse 18). So God will give him Egypt as wages for his army, ‘because it was done for Me’ (verse 20). ‘In that day I will cause a horn to sprout for the house of Israel, and I will open your mouth to speak among them’ (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
This word is dated to the spring of 571 BC. Nebuchadnezzar's long siege of Tyre had ended without the plunder his army expected; the bald heads and raw shoulders picture the hard labor of the siege. A broken Babylonian text seems to record a campaign by Nebuchadnezzar against Egypt about 568 or 567 BC, though its details are uncertain.

The book does not hide that the earlier word about Tyre did not come about as Nebuchadnezzar's plunder. It records the fact, and God's provision for it. A horn is a picture of strength.
passages.later: Isaiah warned that trust in Egypt would end in shame: ‘Pharaoh’s protection will become your shame’ (Isaiah 30:3). Hannah sang that God would ‘exalt the horn of His anointed’ (1 Samuel 2:10).
passages.asks: Ezekiel recorded honestly what had not turned out as expected. Ask whether you can be honest with God when things do not happen the way you thought. And ask what it means that he is still at work.
